title: Spherical Analogue of the Law of Cosines

problemStatement.formal: cos(c) = cos(a)·cos(b) + sin(a)·sin(b)·cos(C) for spherical triangle sides a,b,c and angle C
problemStatement.plain: What is the spherical analogue of the Law of Cosines? For a spherical triangle on the unit sphere with arc-length sides a, b, c and dihedral angle C opposite side c: cos(c) = cos(a)·cos(b) + sin(a)·sin(b)·cos(C).
whyMatters: Fundamental identity in spherical geometry and navigation
Generalizes the planar law of cosines to curved surfaces
Key tool in geodesy, astronomy, and great-circle navigation
Reduces to planar law of cosines in the small-angle limit

proven: Unit vector inner product bounds: |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ 1 for unit u,v (proved in Lean)
Arc length = arccos(⟨u,v⟩) is well-defined, symmetric, non-negative, ≤ π (proved in Lean)
Inner product decomposition: ⟨u,v⟩ = ⟨u,n⟩⟨v,n⟩ + ⟨proj⊥(u,n), proj⊥(v,n)⟩ (proved in Lean)
Spherical law of cosines in algebraic form (proved in Lean)
Spherical law of cosines in trigonometric form (proved in Lean)
knownResults.goal: Formalize the spherical law of cosines using unit vectors in ℝ³ and Mathlib inner product spaces

knowledge.progressSummary: COMPLETED: Created SphericalLawOfCosines.lean with 24 proved theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries. Formalizes the spherical law of cosines using unit vectors in ℝ³ and Mathlib's inner product space infrastructure.
insights: The key algebraic identity is the inner product decomposition: ⟨u,v⟩ = ⟨u,n⟩⟨v,n⟩ + ⟨proj⊥(u,n), proj⊥(v,n)⟩
For unit vectors, this becomes cos(c) = cos(b)cos(a) + ⟨proj⊥(A,C), proj⊥(B,C)⟩
The perpendicular projection proj⊥(v,n) = v - ⟨v,n⟩n has norm equal to sin(arcLength(v,n))
EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) works well as the ambient space for unit sphere geometry
Explicit @inner ℝ Vec3 _ annotations needed for EuclideanSpace type resolution
The proof requires establishing ⟪n,n⟫ and ⟪u,u⟫ as separate facts before the simp/ring chain
builtItems: 5 unit vector theorems (self inner product, bounds, ≤1, ≥-1)
5 arc length theorems (non-neg, ≤π, cos recovery, self=0, symmetry)
SphericalTriangle structure with sides and angle definitions

No Mathlib definition of spherical triangles or dihedral angles
Mathlib has inner product spaces but no spherical geometry built on top
